column1: # title: ENG-205 Midterm — 4 Wife of Bath

column2: The Wife opens by saying her own experience, even without the authority of learned clerks' books, is enough to speak of the woe in marriage.
She has married five times since age twelve: three good, rich, old husbands, a fourth who had a mistress, and a young fifth, Jankin.
Rich old men she controlled through sex, scolding, and false accusations until they gave her their land and gold.
A reveller who kept a mistress; she made him jealous in return, and he died just as she came back from her pilgrimage to Jerusalem.
A twenty-year-old former Oxford clerk she married after the fourth's funeral, giving him all her land, though he beat her.
A collection of stories about wicked wives that he read aloud every night to show that women are evil.
She tears three pages out and punches him into the fire, he hits her so hard she goes deaf in one ear, then he repents, gives her control, and burns the book.
Jankin gives her "the bridle," control of house, land, tongue, and hand, and after that they never argued and she was kind and true to him.
He is a miser who will not let another man light a candle at his lantern, since he loses no light, so a husband loses nothing if she is generous with herself.
She says Venus gave her lust and Mars gave her boldness, so her nature was set by the stars at her birth.
From a fable: a lion seeing a picture of a man killing a lion asks who painted it, meaning that if women wrote the books, men would look far wickeder.
King Arthur's time, long ago, when Britain was full of fairies and the elf-queen danced in the meadows.
The friars, "limitours," now bless every house and field, so the only thing a woman meets in the woods is a friar.
A young knight of Arthur's court rapes a maiden he meets by a river.
Arthur condemns him to death, but the queen spares him if within a year and a day he can find what women most desire.

column1: 16. The answer that saves his life
column2: An old, ugly woman tells him: women most desire sovereignty over their husbands and to have mastery over them.
He must grant the old woman whatever she asks, and she demands that he marry her.
In bed she tells him true nobility comes from virtuous deeds, not birth or wealth, and defends poverty and old age.
Have her old and ugly but faithful, or young and beautiful and risk her unfaithfulness.
He lets her choose, putting himself in her "wise governance," so she has the mastery.
She becomes both beautiful and faithful, they live in joy, and the Wife prays Jesus send meek young husbands and shorten the lives of those not governed by their wives.
